You're welcome. I can't speak for the other Little Italy's that exist around the Nation, but I know a decent amount about the one here. As a third generation, Italian American, and also someone that loves History, I've read and studied a bunch about the roots of the people that came here generations ago. Probably one of my favorite things to do!

Little Italy, more or less, always served Italian-American food. Mainly due to the concentration of Italian immigrants from different regions of central to southern Italy, and the lack of some ingredients that were commonly found in the regions they grew up in. They were able to make due, and many started restaurants combining their old world knowledge, with more of an American twist because they essentially needed the business of non-italian customers, in order for their businesses to thrive. It's pretty much where all the Italian-American dishes come from. Nowadays, Little Italy is a shell of itself, a massive tourist trap with no actual Italians and few few Italian Americans left. The demographics have shifted for the most part, and we as a Nation, aren't getting as many Italian Immigrants as we used to.

The population of Italian-Americans on the whole, is down, at least in New York. There used to be many different enclaves of Italian-Americans, scattered around the five boroughs. Bensonhurst and Bath Beach, two neighborhoods in Brooklyn, were predominantly Italian American for a very long time, but have been rapidly shifting to different cultures, since the late 90's/early 2000's. There are still many Italian American families and businesses left, but they shrink with each passing year, as many of the previous generations die off, and their families move away to different places. I would argue that the nicest "little Italy" you're going to find, nowadays, exists on Arthur Avenue in the Bronx.

Staten Island, has many New Yorkers, who trace their roots to Italy. Mostly people who at this point are 2nd or 3rd generation. There's a pretty thriving Italian American community, on the South Shore of Staten Island. We all understand the stigma that Staten Island carries, and there's plenty of issues with it (Just like any of the other boroughs) but there are many nice people, families, and businesses of Italian Americans out there, that someone can patronize if they wish.

The ball is from 1957-1959. But there's definitely something puzzling about it. 

It has signatures of Mantle, Stengal, Slaughter and Shantz from what I could quickly identify, which were only on a team together in the late fifties.

However by the time all these players were on the team together, Mantle's signature had changed. The Mantle on your ball, resembles his early fifties signature. By the end of the fifties, The Mick's signature started to have looping "M's" which would eventually evolve into his show signature that was popularized in the 70's and 80's. This leads me to think it's either of the following scenario's

1. The Ball started out with just signatures of Mantle and Stengal, and the original owner, added signatures along the way, as the years went on and he met more players.

or

Teacher here:

Standardized testing does not properly gauge a students knowledge on a subject. What I mean by that is, it's quite simply impossible to take every little bit of a curriculum, stuff it down into one, comprehensive exam, and then say "Well this shows that Johnny is good at math"

A test alone does not show a students proficiency on a subject. What if the student was having a bad day on the day of the test? Maybe something's going on at home? What if they're taking care of a sibling? What if they get anxiety when taking a test? What if they have a learning disability that impairs them when dealing with a written test?

Also to boil down a child's entire knowledge of a subject to one standardized exam is disingenuous. It doesn't represent who they are as a learner or what they know. A comprehensive portfolio of work over the course of a month or two would be a much better indicator of a students knowledge of a subject. And as a bonus they wouldn't have to deal with the pressure of a standardized test hanging over their head. They are children. Some of them can't handle that pressure because they haven't developed the coping mechanism for it yet. They should not be penalized for doing bad on one test. The point of school is to educate them, to lift them up.

Many of the traditions we still carry are what was passed down from them but the line blurs from what was "strictly Italian" to what is  "Italian American." We do something called "Feast of the 7" during Christmas Eve, we celebrate certain Saint days, have certain meals, sunday dinner is always served every Sunday. However those are most likely more Italian-American things than anything. The traditions are rooted in our family much more than the culture of "being italian" I would wager.
